speaker: Matt Risinger
title: Building Science with Matt Risinger ECP 66
question: In custom home building, why do many experienced builders avoid competitively bidding out subcontractors on every new project?
guest: We keep the same subs job after job. We treat them like partners in the business. We don't bid them against other people for the most part, and I have an annual negotiation with them about increases in pricing. I have the same HVAC guy I've used in every house I've built in the last 15 or 16 years here in Austin. I've got the same frame carpenter, who also does cornice, exterior trim, and siding, who's worked with me for a dozen years, and two concrete guys who have done all my work for the last dozen years. By having that continuity of really good tradesmen, it also means that I don't need a superintendent at the job every single day to have 30 years of construction background, if I've got the same trades that have always worked with me and know what I expect. With a VP of construction who has been in the business his whole life and trades that have always worked on my houses, I don't have to be at every job every day.

points.core: Builders replace per-job competitive bidding with annual pricing negotiations for trusted trades.
points.note: Accept: negotiating rates once a year with long-term trade partners instead of soliciting competing bids on each house. Do not credit: generic advice about building good relationships without mentioning how pricing/bidding is structured.

points.core: Repeat subcontractors already internalize the builder's quality standards across every new project.
points.note: Accept: multi-year continuity means trades know the builder's exact details, expectations, and methods without retraining on every job. Do not credit: vague claims that loyal subs work harder or care more.

points.core: Trade continuity reduces the need for veteran superintendents with decades of experience.
points.note: Accept: when experienced repeat trades carry institutional knowledge on site, day-to-day project managers or superintendents do not need 20–30 years of hands-on trade background, freeing the owner from daily site presence. Do not credit: generic statements that good subs make management easier without linking to superintendent experience or supervision load.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Experienced custom builders usually prefer a stable roster of trusted subcontractors because the lowest bid rarely produces the lowest total cost or the best house.

Custom homes are one-off projects with incomplete or evolving plans, so bids from unfamiliar subs are hard to compare on equal terms. A low bidder often has missed scope, plans to recover margin through change orders, or will cut corners on quality and staffing. A sub the builder knows already understands their standards, details, and expectations. That means less supervision, fewer mistakes and callbacks, and more reliable pricing.

Relationships also buy things a bid can't. Loyal subs prioritize a repeat builder's jobs when labor is tight, show up on schedule, coordinate smoothly with the other trades they've worked alongside before, and come back to handle warranty issues without a fight. They also offer early budgeting help and honest pricing during design, which they won't do for builders who just shop their numbers.

Finally, bidding every job is time-consuming, and good subs stop responding to builders who constantly use them as price checks. Most builders instead spot-check pricing periodically to keep their regular subs competitive.

The candidate explicitly says familiar subcontractors already know the builder’s standards and project details.

points.why: The candidate mentions less supervision without explaining how repeat trades reduce the need for a superintendent with decades of experience.

Unique plans inevitably contain intricate details and scope gaps; unfamiliar low bidders often miss items up front, then recover thin margins by cutting corners or charging steep change orders. Vetted subcontractors, by contrast, already understand the builder’s craftsmanship standards, jobsite expectations, and sequencing, allowing adjacent trades to coordinate smoothly with minimal rework.

Loyalty also secures scarce skilled labor. Top tradespeople prioritize builders who offer steady, fair work—showing up on schedule, helping refine preconstruction budgets, and promptly handling warranty callbacks after move-in. Constantly shopping bids alienates the best crews, who eventually stop spending unpaid hours estimating or pad their quotes, leaving the builder with less dependable labor. Instead, seasoned builders keep costs fair by checking proposals against historical unit pricing and periodically benchmarking the market.

noweb.answer:
Experienced custom home builders avoid competitively bidding every project because the lowest upfront price rarely delivers the lowest total cost or the required craftsmanship. Custom homes involve complex, one-off details where trade coordination and execution matter far more than shaving a few percent off a bid. Unvetted low bidders frequently recover thin margins through aggressive change orders, cut corners, or cause costly schedule delays and rework.

Working repeatedly with a core group of trusted subcontractors creates predictability and efficiency. Familiar trades already understand the builder’s quality standards, jobsite expectations, and how to coordinate seamlessly with one another—such as framers, plumbers, and HVAC crews anticipating each other’s needs—which sharply reduces supervision overhead and costly mistakes.

Finally, loyalty is a two-way street. Top-tier trades rarely waste time pricing complex custom plans if their numbers are constantly shopped around. By paying fair, market-checked rates rather than chasing the bottom dollar, builders earn scheduling priority when labor is tight, honest feedback during preconstruction, and dependable support on punch lists and warranty callbacks long after closing.

Experienced custom builders usually value long-term trade partnerships more than winning the lowest price on each job. In custom work, quality, reliability and communication matter more than a small difference in a bid. A plumber or framer who has worked with the builder for years knows their standards, details, scheduling habits and clients' expectations. That cuts down on mistakes, rework, callbacks and supervision time, and those hidden costs often outweigh whatever a lower bid saves.

Bidding every job also tends to attract the lowest bidder, who may cut corners, leave out scope, or make up the margin later through change orders. Loyal subs, by contrast, tend to show up when they're needed, put the builder's jobs first when everyone is busy, fix problems without a fight, and price fairly because they expect steady repeat work. Running a full bid process on every project also takes a lot of estimating time on both sides, and good trades get tired of bidding work they rarely win.

Many builders handle this by checking prices against the market now and then, or by negotiating openly with their core subs, instead of re-bidding everything.
